285.history: The fishing town on the eastern cape kept a driftwood fire to bring its boats home in a storm long before the strangers came, and Torcall Clachair laid his second cairn there in the sixth year with James Fenn beside him. When A' Chompanaidh raised Taigh-solais Baile ìseal in the twenty-seventh year, the lime for its mortar was burned on the shore with coal carted over the hills from Muileann chrom, and the keeping of the lamp went to the fishing households, who drew lots for the watches at Samhain as they had for the fire. The custodians won a rule that the lamp be lowered on the nights the boats went to the deep grounds, and the old fire was still lit beside the tower.

136.history: The city of the white sand lay below the dunes of Cuan ruadh. Peter Voss, a glazier of A' Chompanaidh who would not take passage home when his contract ended, built a glass-house there in the sixty-sixth year and melted the sand with charcoal from the hills. His first three firings gave only a black slag that the children carried off for luck; the fourth gave a pale green pane, and his apprentice Cairistìona nic Griogair laughed at the sight of a gull through it. It was the first glass made on Dia-thìr, and the town's apprentices were blowing it without him within a generation. Its custodians were among those of the east whose petitions against the coal tally in the drought went unanswered.

31.history: The hill town south of the coal country got its pits in the thirty-seventh year, with Seumas Dubh of Raghnall Maor's crews set over them as overseer. A year later the haulage rope parted under three full tubs and crushed Coinneach Beag, a boy of eleven, and the crew killed Seumas Dubh for the haste he had ordered. A' Chompanaidh hanged two hewers, Eòin Ruadh and Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, at Ros dhomhain, the first hanging done by Riaghaltas nan Coigreach on Dia-thìr. The town's roll names the boy, his age and his mother, and the two hanged men, whom their neighbours carried home and buried in the town's own ground.

9.history: The Tuathaich harbour town of the north coast ate its seed corn in the second winter of Gorta Baile chrom, and was fed through that season by the kitchen of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise at the harbour, three hundred a day on fish broth and biscuit brought by sea from Cathair gheal. Its landing was walled by the humans. In the last year of the age the seven of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe lay twelve hours in a boat-shed there, heard that Strake's constables rode the western roads daily, and hired a carter of the town with a covered cart and a mule who asked nothing of what he carried.
9.known_for: the harbour kitchen of the hunger

418.history: The ford town on the northern road kept a carters' house at its quay that stood roofless for most of the age. Muireall nic Fhearchair, carrying her aunt's papers east to the loft at Muileann chaol in the thirtieth year, was held there by rain and read Clàr nan Dà Fhichead Dath aloud to the carters. That same autumn the town's carter, Seònaid Bhàn's father, lodged the drivers and oxen of the meal-carts of Doire fhiadhaich. Seònaid married Pàdraig mac Artair of Doire chaol there, took the old carters' house, and made her rule of marks and barter at its table.

22.history: The river-mouth city of the south coast was where A' Chompanaidh's ships loaded the coal that came down the Abhainn uaine from Seann Toll, and went out by Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich. Its fishermen netted the last salmon of the green river's mouth in the thirty-third year, a hen fish empty of eggs; the next spring none came in from the sea, their gravel under the grey slurry of the washing-floors. In the thirty-sixth year a coal ship on the ebb ran down one of its boats off the bar and did not stop, and after that the town's boats kept inshore.

241.history: The farming town of the east lost its seed corn in the ground in the forty-eighth year and borrowed seed from A' Chompanaidh's store at Seann Dunn, to be paid back in grain over five harvests. Tormod mac Pheadair, keeper of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg and kin of the town by marriage, walked there to read the terms to its council figure by figure. The custodians entered the debt under the night of the moon with its measure and its five harvests, the first debt in grain to the strangers in any roll of the island.

301.history: The small harbour on the northern coast took in the crew of a brig of A' Chompanaidh wrecked in sea mist off Eilean fhada in the fifty-fifth year; they waded ashore at low water and walked there. A' Chompanaidh built a quay at the town for the eastern trade, and by the hundred and forty-fifth year it saw one ship in a season. Its agent wrote to Ros dhomhain that he had been forgotten, and no answer came back to him that Rathad na Mèinne ever heard of.

436.history: The town of the eastern drought country was kept through Tiormachd Achadh shean by its custodian Iseabail nic Leòid. In the hundred and seventh year she drove the herds of Àth mhòr and Achadh shean a day west to the tarn above Doire fhionn, and fewer than half the beasts reached water on their own legs; she kept a count of the fallen, ninety-eight marks. Of the ten drought custodians who petitioned Haskins, each unknown to the others, she rode her own petition to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and over the following winter wrote forty pages on the three dry years. Haskins answered in two lines, and a later clerk bound the two together.

308.history: The village of the grasslands in the western hills lay off every road but the one from Ros bheag to the northern concession. In the last year of the age the seven of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe lay eleven hours in the long grass above that road and counted every rider who passed, Gillebrìde keeping the tally on a strip of bark: forty-one constables' riders in a day, all going south and none north.

192.history: The city above Seann Toll on the northern coast sent its first wool south to the humans' post by coasting boat in the third year, and its custodians took their payment in paper and ink and began the town's roll afresh with them. Thomas Pike added a quire of his own writing-paper uncounted, the one line of the post's first tally-book he did not balance, and marked it as a gift.
192.known_for: the roll begun on the strangers' paper

145.history: The village in the hills north of the workings kept Na Seann Spioradan, and its households would not light their hearths with coal bought of A' Chompanaidh; they burned peat as their grandparents had, and their elders taught that coal burned for wages was burned twice. Fionnghal nic Artair rode there in an Giblean of the twenty-third year and read her letter in defence of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig at the hearth of Sìleas nic Uilleim. Asked what burned on her own hearth, she answered bought coal, and was sent home with thanks.
145.known_for: the hearths that burned no bought coal

450.history: The quay town on the Abhainn ìseal gave its name to Seòlaid Ceann òg, the traders' lane that ran down the river past Cnoc bheag and Inis bhàn, west along the north coast and round the western capes to the capital. In the autumn of the twenty-ninth year A' Chompanaidh shipped the fishers and net-menders whose foreshores it had bought up that lane to Ceann òg and walked them over the hills to the pits.

296.history: The villages of the south sent meal north to the hill villages in the hungry thirty-first year, as the custom of An Aois Naomh bids. The agents of A' Chompanaidh at Àth ìseal bought two of the nine carts on the road; the seven that refused their marks went on into the hills and gave their meal away sack by sack at the village doors, as Lagh a' Bhìdh Roinnte bids, and their drivers came home by the carriers' road with their carts empty.

126.history: The fishing town on the southern shore sheltered the crew of A' Chompanaidh's collier when the raiders burned her in the forty-sixth year and set her men rowing for the land; its households fed them until a rider could carry word south. The next year a gunboat of A' Chompanaidh hunted the raiders to a cove near the town and burned every boat drawn up on the shingle, most of them its own fishermen's. The raiders were not found.

118.history: The city of the north-west kept a hall of disputation of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. In the forty-ninth year students of Aonghas mac Coinnich carried his question there, why the humans cannot see the colour in broken coal, and the hall argued it until its record ran to four hundred leaves. The last leaf lists those who spoke and notes that the hall adjourned because the peat was done.

142.history: In the fiftieth year human farmers of the concession cleared land beside the Tuathaich village of the upland north-west and built a mill; through the first winter the villagers sold them grain at a fair price and carried it on their own ponies, and when the farmers' mill turned in the spring they sold no more and gave no reason.
142.known_for: the grain sold for one winter

358.history: The weaving town of the north took a contract of A' Chompanaidh for canvas for the camp tents and sacks for the coal in the sixty-eighth year, by a vote of twenty-six to nine against its eldest weaver, Ealasaid Bhuidhe, who signed the roll of dissent and then wove canvas with the rest. The town throve on it. Its custodians noted that never before had it made anything for a use it did not approve.

204.history: In the wool city of the western coast a fleece had been the measure of every bargain until Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's table of the eighty-sixth year made it worth what a half-fleece had been before. The weavers stopped bringing wool to the humans' market and loaded it for their own crossing instead, and A' Chompanaidh, holding the only deep-water berths on that coast, let it lie until the moths had most of it.
204.known_for: the wool left to the moths

191.history: The harbour town of the south-west paid its dues in fish until they were called in marks in the eighty-third year. They could be raised no way but by selling boats: eleven of its two-and-twenty went to A' Chompanaidh at its own asking price, and the men who sailed them went into the pits under the next year's contracts. Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, the lane the coal ships took west along the south coast, is named for its strait.

347.history: The eastern port got a customs house of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach in the ninety-eighth year and a store of A' Chompanaidh with it, opened as help against a bad year. The store sold the east its seed and its tools, and within a few years its ledgers held the debts of half the district, entered against named households; Coinneach Òg told the custodians so at the fire inside the wall of Ceann àrsaidh when they met to draft the petition. Baile ruadh borrowed its seed corn there in the drought.

311.history: The cattle town of the east had no grazing left within four days' driving in the second summer of Tiormachd Achadh shean, and its custodian Ealasaid Ruadh ordered the whole herd killed and salted rather than lose it on the road. The salt meat was sold to A' Chompanaidh for the camps at a price A' Chompanaidh named. The town lost fewer of its people to hunger that winter than any other in the drought country.

449.history: The farm village of the north-east lost its grazing two years running in the drought, and sent its young to sign hewers' contracts at Cnoc fhiadhaich and elsewhere, the first villagers of the eastern farm country to go to the pits for wages. Families who had kept beasts and small fields for generations went down in a single season, and their custodian wrote it down as the end of the village, not a flitting.

127.history: The harbour town on Eilean ruadh became in the hundred and twenty-third year the seat of the district of the outer coasts, ruled from its harbour office, where the revenue cutters of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach lay. Its surveyors walked the edge of the great moss beyond the town, found no way across, and left the rest of the district's map blank; the custodians of those coasts were no readier to be counted than the moss.

196.history: The small northern town shares its name with the town of the cellar, and in the hundred and twenty-fifth year three years of copies bound for the cellar came to it by mistake. Its old custodian kept them whole and dry, and when Cailean mac Eachainn walked north to fetch them he said only that a roll is a roll, and that he had kept it well until someone came to say it was theirs.

324.history: The fishing village below Am Buabhall Fortanach became in the war years the landing for goods the great road-house could not take by road. Its fishermen, old Coinneach nan Ràmh among them, took to being paid for certain nights never spoken of as work in silver struck in an Tìr Thall rather than the coin of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, and none of it was spent where a clerk of A' Chompanaidh might see.

2.history: The river port just east of the capital stacked on its quays the coal that the barges carried down the Abhainn fhionn to A' Chompanaidh's steamships at Cathair dhomhain. In the last year of the age its townsfolk set the stacks alight rather than let a ship carry them off to burn against another Seann Toll, and the ships put in at Ros dhomhain and burned their own stores. The word reached the muster of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe at Seann Skell.

365.history: The weaving city of the northern coast traded its cloth for the humans' dyes in the fourth year, a red and a blue brighter than any the island could make, and within a few years the old madder fields about the town went back to grass.

493.history: The herders' village under Binnean a' Chlachair, the highest ground of the island, refused James Fenn a night fire on the summit in the sixth year, keeping the custom of the hills. Torcall Clachair laid one stone on the herders' cairn there, and Fenn took his fire to the headlands instead.

420.history: The coastal town a day's walk up from Cuan shean took Fiabhras nan Coigreach in the tenth year, which killed its custodian and both her sons, though no human dwelt in the town at all. The custodians of the west took note of it.

45.history: The fishing town whose boats had anchored free at Ros dhomhain time out of mind was charged anchorage under Puingean a' Chalaidh in the twentieth year. Having paid it once, its fishermen took their catch to their own jetty and sold it there to the fish-wives who walked out from the capital and to anyone but A' Chompanaidh, whose salting-house had herring that season only from its own boats.
45.known_for: herring sold to anyone but A' Chompanaidh

316.history: The village of the south kept the old count of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig, the measure of coal that might be burned in a year, one season longer than any other town on the island, and entered it in its roll with the note that no one asked for it.
316.known_for: the last count of the old law

273.history: The city on the river road grew, as the coal came down to it from Cidhe Beag, into the busiest barge town of the north. Its people doubled in number in the thirties, most of the newcomers bargemen from the coast.

164.history: The carters of the village on the road just east of the capital banded together in the thirty-fifth year to bargain with A' Chompanaidh over the rates for hauling coal, the first Dia-thìreach guild of the age; A' Chompanaidh bought it, because that was cheaper than breaking it. Pàdraig mac Artair, who married Seònaid Bhàn of Cuan chrom, was a carter of the town, and its carters swore at Seònaid's table.

106.history: The southern town took A' Bhreac Bhallach when it spread south from the harbour in the fortieth year, and its custodians cut the names of the dead into the stone lintel of the council house, where they can still be read.

232.history: The carters of the south-western town took up the carrying of Seann Warr brine-salt round the lake to the capital in the forty-fifth year, a trade A' Chompanaidh did not trouble to claim; Comann an Airgid entered the salt in its ledger. The trade kept the town's folk out of the pits for the whole of the age.

92.history: The town a day's sail east of Baile dhìreach took in the human boatbuilders when they moved their yard there in the forty-seventh year for the timber A' Chompanaidh had promised them, and it made no joint council and no compact with them. Iain Hale refused the yard and stayed at Baile dhìreach. Within a generation the boatbuilders faded from the town's rolls.

62.history: The river town took the eastern coal, carted over the rebuilt bridge at Ros fhionn and down to its quays, and sent it by barge to Caol chrom at the river mouth for shipping. A' Chompanaidh deepened the river at the quays in the fifty-third year, and the town's old fish market was moved to make room.

144.history: The quays below Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag took the eastern coal that Inis bheag could not load. Its townsfolk were paid by the barge, and with the gain the town built its first stone houses.

443.history: The road for the eastern coal to Inis bheag passed the town by a mile in the fifty-fourth year, and it got only the dust of the traffic it had hoped for. Its custodians wrote that they had not known a town could be harmed by a road it was not on.
443.known_for: the road it was not on

113.history: Human fishermen of the concession taught the boats of the north-coast town to hunt whales with the hand-lance in the fifty-fifth year rather than wait for them to strand. The oil was sold to A' Chompanaidh for its lamps, and from then on whale-boats went out from the north coast every summer.

148.history: After A' Chompanaidh's surveyors were lost on the high ground in the fifty-sixth year the people of the village at the foot of the hills left salt and coal for the sìth, as their grandparents had after any death there. A' Chompanaidh forbade coal to be left lying and had the offerings gathered up. The search party that went up after the surveyors came back with nothing but the tale of the Marbh-bheò.

290.history: The city under Cnoc naomh was where the tithe-gatherers began in the fifty-eighth year to weigh grain as well as coal, saying the town's farms fed the pits and shared in their gain. Griogair Fada, the largest farmer under the hill, asked the young gatherer who had set the new weight and got no answer he could carry home. The custodians entered the weighing in their roll under a name of their own coining, the tithe on the tithe.

162.history: The river port east of the capital on the Abhainn fhionn took An Scàird Fhuilteach from the coal barges in the sixtieth year, after a sick bargeman was put ashore there. Its custodians, led by Mairead nic Amhlaidh, shut the only barge landing the town had for a whole season, though it cost every fee the landing had ever earned; A' Chompanaidh fined the town for the lost fees, and Mairead read the letter to the council on the landing steps within sight of that season's graves.

30.history: The city of the south got A' Chompanaidh's pay office for the southern workings in the sixty-first year, when Crane moved it there from the pit-heads. The crews of every southern pit walked a day there and a day back twice a month to be paid, with no pay for the walking; Uisdean Ruadh of Muileann chrom kept the cost of it on a notched stick.

187.history: The town in the hills, not the town of that name in the north-west, took A' Phlàigh Uaine in the seventy-fourth year. The scribes kept the two apart with care, for the tellings of the island's hungers confuse them.

501.history: After A' Phlàigh Uaine the people of the town, who had worked the southern galleries, left their camp huts and went back to the old village on the hill. The next year A' Chompanaidh built the huts again and brought in crews from the west.

90.history: The fishermen of the southern harbour town carried salt fish up to the camps by night in the years of Sìol-lann na Companaidh, past its ration and its rule. The custodians' roll calls it the only trade of that decade that ran the right way.

306.history: The Tuathaich town sent forty-one of its people to the pits under An Togail, the largest tally of any single town. Nineteen came back when their term was done; the custodians' roll names the other twenty-two and the camps they were carried to, four with no camp given at all.

247.history: The custodians of the town offered the officers of An Togail silver in the eighty-ninth year to halve its tally. The officers weighed the purse, kept it as an offering to A' Chompanaidh's granary, and read the whole list uncut. The complaint was lodged at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and filed, and no other town on record offered a bribe after it.

333.history: The village of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean north of the eastern workings held the schools' last open disputation on its threshing-floor on the eve of Bealltainn in the ninetieth year, before three parishes' folk, on whether a question may rightly be forbidden. The clerk of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach who attended noted that it may.

119.history: The harbour town of the eastern shore had carried goods by day along a coast too dangerous to run by night. When Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh was finished in the ninety-first year, A' Chompanaidh's steamers rounded the island without putting in, and the town's coasting boats were laid up within a few years. Voss's white sand came from its dunes.

328.history: Gorta Baile chrom reached as far east as the village in the ninety-sixth year. Its custodians levered open the sealed grain-pits of An Aois Naomh on the chalk hill above the town, unopened in living memory and kept against a need no one thought would come, and found in them only dust.

397.history: A second deep-water quay was built at the village in the south-east in the hundred and third year for the eastern coal, by builders brought from the coast, and a village of forty houses became a town of four hundred.

117.history: The village of the eastern drought country had its tarn fouled by the driven cattle of every drought district within a week of the drive, and its women walked each day to the spring at Àth ruadh and back for water, half a day's journey. The custodians recorded it for the three dry years, and then ceased.

103.history: Pilgrims of Na Seann Spioradan bound for the spring of Allt an Àigh, which never failed through the three dry years, gathered at the town, and its folk fed them freely, as Na Seann Spioradan require, and opened their own granary to them rather than see them go hungry on the road home. Its wells were low, and it gave away more water than it kept.

424.history: The drought-fever spread to the town from Baile Mòr ruadh in the hundred and ninth year and took mostly the very young. Its one well was found tainted and closed, and for a year the town drank from carts.

151.history: The old barter market at the ford, where hill and coast had met to trade since An Aois Naomh, closed after a poor last season in the hundred and thirtieth year, when barter was struck down, and the green shoulder of ground above the ford stood empty from then on.

160.history: The Tuathaich mill town of the north-west shut its roads against Am Fiabhras Glas in the hundred and forty-first year and kept them shut a season, turning the concession's human carters back at the town's edge with their loads still on the carts. No custodian there ordered it, and every custodian there defended it.
160.known_for: the roads shut against the fever

435.history: Am Fiabhras Glas took one household in three at the northern village in the hundred and forty-first year. Its custodians burned no huts; they had heard of Àth ghlas in their grandparents' time, but judged it too late.

240.history: The workings of the north-eastern town among the druid villages stopped with the rest on Là Stad nan Sloc, the day of the fire. Its custodian wrote that it was the first thing the town had done with the hills in a hundred years.
240.known_for: the first thing done with the hills

175.history: The pits north of the hills at the town stopped with the rest on Là Stad nan Sloc, the word brought by a runner and not by the beacon. Their crew-leaders were among the eight shipped over the sea when the stoppage was broken, and never heard of again.

42.history: The coal stage of the northern-coast town stopped loading on Là Stad nan Sloc. Its dockers had not been told; they stopped because the coal stopped coming.

262.history: The quarrymen of the north-eastern town, who cut stone for A' Chompanaidh's buildings, laid down their tools on Là Stad nan Sloc unasked. Why, no one said.

131.history: The crews of the northern pit town rose in the same week as the other northern pits in the hundred and forty-ninth year, took the constable posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, and sent the constables south on foot. Their crew-leaders had left a cairn of spoil-stones, one from each pit, on the moor above Cnoc naomh the night they fixed the week.

137.history: The river port just east of the capital argued three days over the war, as much on trade as on loyalty, and then sent its boats to the council at Cathair dhearg. Through that winter and the next the boats carried food down the Abhainn fhionn to the capital by night.
137.known_for: the boats sent to the council

167.history: Riflemen raised at the eastern town joined the companies of Comann an Airgid in Cogadh nam Beann and held the eastern road. A' Chompanaidh's carters caught on it were let go home with their carts.
167.known_for: the riflemen of the eastern road

57.history: The city of the eastern workings stood by the rebuilt bridge on the eastern coal road. In Cogadh nam Beann its crews stopped the pumps and walked out, and the lower galleries flooded; A' Chompanaidh's engineers went down the Abhainn chaol and took ship at Seann Mhorn for Ros dhomhain, and the bridge fell silent.

36.history: Fishing boats of the southern town and of Ros ruadh, sailing by night along the south coast in the last year of the age, boarded a coaster of A' Chompanaidh at anchor and burned her, and A' Chompanaidh drew its coastal shipping back to the harbours of Ros dhomhain and Ros bheag.

14.history: The fishermen of the other Seann Chwen, further west on the south coast, joined the raids along the shore in the last year of the age. The rolls tell the two towns apart by the names of their boats.

54.history: The Tuathaich town of the concession blocked its road with carts in Cogadh nam Beann and kept a watch on it against both sides. No one attacked it, and the watch was kept to the end of the war.

128.history: The farming town of the south-east, not the salt port of that name in the west, sent grain to the hills by the eastern roads from the first winter of Cogadh nam Beann, and the council's roll lists the carts; Dùghall of the harbour quarter counted them at Ros dhomhain.

392.history: In the hills beyond the capital, the guards of A' Chompanaidh and the constables sallying from the capital's harbour to win back the eastern road were driven back at the town in the last year of the age, in Blàr Cnoc ghorm. It was the last attempt Riaghaltas nan Coigreach made in the war to reach the mining district.

104.history: The river quays of the city east of the capital opened to the council's boats in the last year of the age. With them and the harbour quarter of Ros dhomhain both lost, Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir could be fed only by water, up the Abhainn gheal from the sea.
104.known_for: the quays opened to the council

122.history: Strake posted constables at the town north of Ros bheag in the last year of the age to hold the coast road, Ceum Ros àrsaidh. The townsfolk brought them food and news, and the news was always a day old.
